## Two very different ways this repo reads gamedata

1. **Offline, dev-tool-only** (`converter.html`, `explorer.html`,
   `assembly.html`, `sprite-editor.html`'s reference importer): standalone
   pages for inspecting/exporting real pack data, not part of any build
   step. Only `converter.html` still picks a pack directory via
   `showDirectoryPicker()` — `explorer.html` and `assembly.html` instead
   fetch `gamedata/` directly over HTTP (an `HttpDirFileProvider`/plain
   `fetch()`, the same access pattern item 2's live-decode modules use),
   so both work straight off the served repo with no folder-picker step.
   `converter.html`'s directory-picker path used to be how the game got
   essentially everything — level terrain, placed objects, the level
   editor's palette art — but that's no longer true for level *data* at
   all, for any rating (see item 2). What's left on this path is exported
   *art* — `levels/{gfx,ani,doors,traps}/*.gif` (object/decoration
   sprites; `src/decorations.js` still fetches these as static files for
   the one case its live-decode `liveRef` mechanism can't cover yet, a
   VGASPEC level's palette-substituted objects — see
   `docs/gif-to-gamedata-migration.md`) — plus `converter.html`'s continued
   role as a standalone diagnostic/export tool. `assembly.html` is a
   newer, unrelated dev tool: an exploded-assembly viewer that flies a
   real level's decoded terrain/object pieces onto a canvas one at a time
   for visual ground-truth checking (`src/assemblyEngine.js`); its
   DOM-independent decode/compositing core is shared live with
   `game.html`'s own level-"prepare" screen (item 2, below), not just used
   offline — see `docs/assembly.md` for the full writeup of both.
   `gamedata/2-players/`'s pre-converted `2-player_level*.js`/
   `codebase/cb_amiga_two_player_*.js` files (converter.html's former
   output for `2-player`) are now dead — see `docs/2-player-dos-assets.md`.

2. **Live, in the actual running app**: `src/mainDatCatalog.js` fetches a
   pack's `MAIN.DAT` directly over HTTP and decodes it in the browser, on
   the fly (rating badges/`src/menu.js`, the scrolling banner/
   `src/scroller.js`). `src/groundCatalog.js` does the same for
   `GROUND<n>O.DAT`+`VGAGR<n>.DAT` (terrain/object art — used by both the
   level editor's palette and `src/gamedataLevelLoader.js`, see below) —
   and, for the pause menu's Video Mode setting, for the CGA/EGA/Tandy
   variants of that same art too (real `CGAGR<n>.DAT` for CGA, the
   embedded `ega_standard`/`ega_preview` palette for EGA, a VGA-palette-swap for Tandy —
   see the `CGAGR{n}.DAT`/EGA/Tandy bullet above); `src/lemmingSpriteCatalog.js`
   does the equivalent for lemming sprites, including the real, separately
   stored `cgamain.dat` for CGA mode. `src/gamedataMusicPlayer.js` and
   `src/tandyAudioEngine.js` decode `ADLIB.DAT`/`TANDYSND.DAT` respectively
   for both music (Music Engine setting) and sound effects (Sound FX
   Engine setting) — see the `ADLIB.DAT`/`TANDYSND.DAT` bullets above.
   `src/gamedataLevelLoader.js` goes furthest for level data: it decodes a
   real level's `LEVEL<n>.DAT`/`DLVEL<n>.DAT` directly — terrain piece
   placement, object placement, steel areas, metadata — and bakes it into
   the same shape `src/terrain.js`/`src/decorations.js` already knew how to
   render for the level editor's custom levels, so real gameplay for every
   rating no longer depends on a pre-converted level script at all —
   including `2-player`, once the one genuine gap ("Extending this
   further" below, before it was closed) — a committed, redistributable
   raw two-player level source — was found and added
   (`gamedata/Amiga-Two-Player/Level NN.lvl`, see
   `docs/2-player-dos-assets.md`). `2-player` reads that raw source
   directly (`loadTwoPlayerLevelFromGamedata()`, no `FileContainer`
   unpack needed — each level is already its own uncompressed file) but
   sources its style/object art from `gamedata/lemmings` rather than
   `gamedata/Amiga-Two-Player`'s own bundled (and byte-identical) copies of
   the same files, to avoid fetching the same bytes twice under two names.
   `src/assemblyEngine.js` shares a further real-decode path (terrain +
   object piece assembly) between `assembly.html` (item 1's offline
   viewer) and `game.html`'s own level-"prepare" screen
   (`src/prepareScreen.js`, shown between levels) — the same live pieces,
   not a separately-baked preview asset.

Both approaches decode through the *same* underlying primitives
(`FileContainer` in `src/datContainer.js`, `PaletteImage`/`ColorPalette` in
`src/planarImage.js`/`src/colorPalette.js` — native ports of the formerly-
vendored `LemmingsJS/js/lemmings.js`, since removed from this repo), so
there's exactly one proven implementation of the DOS decompression +
planar-bitmap decode algorithms in this repo, not two.

## `MAIN.DAT`

`docs/lemmings_main_dat_file_format.txt` (by ccexplore and Mindless) is the
authoritative byte-level reference. Once decompressed, `MAIN.DAT` splits
into 7 sections (`FileContainer.getPart(0..6)`):

| Section | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Lemming walk/dig/climb/etc. sprite animations |
| 1 | Terrain-destruction masks (bash/mine/explode) + explosion-countdown digit font |
| 2 | "High-performance" (PS/2) mode skill panel + fonts |
| 3 | Main menu: brown background, Lemmings logo, F1–F4/rating/exit signs — **including the "Level Rating sign" plaque** at `0xBF6C` (120×61px, 4bpp) |
| 4 | Main menu continued: blinking-eye animations, **the scroller's working-lemming sprites + reel tile + purple text font**, and **the 4 base per-rating signs** (72×27px, 4bpp) |
| 5 | Unknown/unused |
| 6 | Standard-mode skill panel + font (same content as section 2, different machine mode) |

Section 4's documented layout (this doc's section 7):

```
0x2A00   left Lemming working scroller   16 frames, 48x16, 4bpp
0x4200   right Lemming working scroller  16 frames, 48x16, 4bpp
0x5A00   reel (tiled to form the belt)    1 frame,  16x16, 4bpp
0x5A80   mayhem-slot rating sign          1 frame,  72x27, 4bpp
0x5E4C   taxing-slot rating sign          1 frame,  72x27, 4bpp
0x6218   tricky-slot rating sign          1 frame,  72x27, 4bpp
0x65E4   fun-slot rating sign             1 frame,  72x27, 4bpp
0x69B0   purple font, '!' (ASCII 33)      1 frame,  16x16, 3bpp
 ...      one glyph every 0x60 bytes, through '~' (ASCII 126)
```

The menu screens use a fixed 16-color palette (this doc's section 2) that
is **not stored in `MAIN.DAT` itself** — it's a hardcoded engine constant,
identical for every pack, reproduced as `MENU_PALETTE_RGB` in
`src/mainDatCatalog.js`.

### Getting the offset table right

The four "rating sign" slots above are labelled `mayhem`/`taxing`/`tricky`/
`fun` because that's what the *original* Lemmings' `MAIN.DAT` puts there —
the doc is written only for that one game. Every other pack reuses the
exact same 7-section structure and the exact same four byte offsets within
section 4, but with **different pixel content** at each slot (a different
rating's name, rendered in that same 72×27 box). None of this was assumed:
every pack's actual `MAIN.DAT` was decoded and the result visually
inspected (a wrong offset decodes to visibly scrambled noise; a right one
decodes to crisp, legible art — an easy and reliable way to confirm byte
offsets empirically rather than trust-and-hope).

What that turned up, beyond what the doc covers:

- **Oh No! More Lemmings has a 5th rating**, and its `MAIN.DAT` reflects
  that: `0x5A80`→HAVOC, `0x5E4C`→WICKED, `0x6218`→WILD, `0x65E4`→CRAZY (same
  four slots, same order/difficulty mapping as the original), plus a **5th
  sign — TAME — appended right after**, at `0x69B0`: exactly where the
  purple-font glyph table starts in the original 4-rating layout. Its
  section 4 is measurably 972 bytes larger than the original's (37052 vs.
  36080 bytes) — exactly one 72×27×4bpp sign's worth (`72*27*4/8 = 972`) —
  confirming the extra sign is *appended*, not inserted earlier and
  shifting everything after it.
- **The "Level Rating sign" plaque frame (section 3, `0xBF6C`) is pixel-
  identical across every pack** — same green plaque, same lemmings, same
  baked-in "FUN" placeholder text (per the doc, this base plaque always
  shows "FUN"; the real per-rating text is always a separate sign drawn on
  top from section 4, replacing just the rectangle-board area). Confirmed
  by decoding `lemmings/` and `oh-no-more-lemmings/`'s copies and comparing
  pixels. `getRatingPlaqueUrl()` therefore only ever decodes it from one
  pack (`lemmings/`), regardless of which rating is actually showing.
- **Holiday Lemmings 93's unused slots aren't blank** — its own
  `mayhem`/`taxing` slots decode to "HAVOC"/"WICKED" (real Oh No! art,
  apparently left over from a shared build template), even though those
  ratings don't exist in a Holiday-93 install. Harmless, since only the
  `fun` slot (FLURRY) and `tricky` slot (BLITZ) are ever actually
  referenced for this pack — but worth knowing before trusting an
  unfamiliar pack's "unused" slots at face value.
- **Holiday Lemmings 94's `MAIN.DAT` is fully self-contained**: all 4 slots
  are populated with real, distinct art — `fun`→"Frost'94", `tricky`→
  "Hail'94", `taxing`→"Flurry93", `mayhem`→"Blitz'93" — meaning the 94
  pack's own file already carries the *reissued* 93 ratings too. There was
  no need to also load Holiday 93's `MAIN.DAT` to render all 4 of Holiday
  94's rating options.
- **`xmaslem91`'s `fun` slot decodes to "CRAZY"** — again, harmless leftover
  art from an unrelated build, not a real Xmas Lemmings rating. This pack's
  ratings intentionally have no `RATING_DAT_SOURCE` entry in `src/menu.js`
  and fall back to the plain-text tile, exactly as they did before this
  change.

The confirmed mapping now lives in `src/menu.js` as `RATING_SIGN_OFFSET`
(the four base byte offsets, keyed by their *original*-game meaning) and
`RATING_DAT_SOURCE` (which pack + which of those offsets each of this
project's rating slugs actually uses):

const RATING_DAT_SOURCE = {
  fun:        { pack: 'lemmings',            offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.fun },
  tricky:     { pack: 'lemmings',            offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.tricky },
  taxing:     { pack: 'lemmings',            offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.taxing },
  mayhem:     { pack: 'lemmings',            offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.mayhem },
  crazy:      { pack: 'oh-no-more-lemmings', offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.fun },
  wild:       { pack: 'oh-no-more-lemmings', offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.tricky },
  wicked:     { pack: 'oh-no-more-lemmings', offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.taxing },
  havoc:      { pack: 'oh-no-more-lemmings', offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.mayhem },
  tame:       { pack: 'oh-no-more-lemmings', offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.tame },
  flurry93:   { pack: 'HLemm93',             offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.fun },
  blizzard93: { pack: 'HLemm93',             offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.tricky },
  frost:      { pack: 'HLemm94',             offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.fun },
  hail:       { pack: 'HLemm94',             offset: RATING_SIGN_OFFSET.tricky },

## `src/mainDatCatalog.js` — the live decode module

This is the one place in the live app (as opposed to the offline dev
tools) that reads `gamedata/` directly. Shape:

- Imports `FileContainer`/`PaletteImage`/`ColorPalette` etc. directly from
  their native `src/*.js` modules (no lazy `<script>` injection or global —
  this used to lazily inject `LemmingsJS/js/lemmings.js` via an
  `ensureLemmingsJs()` helper and read off `window.Lemmings`; that vendored
  directory has since been fully ported to native ES modules and deleted
  from the repo, so every consumer, including `converter.html`/
  `explorer.html`, now imports these modules directly instead).
- **`loadMainDat(pack)`** — fetches `gamedata/<pack>/<filename>`, where
  `filename` comes from `src/gamedataPacks.js`'s `mainDatFilename(pack)`
  (case matters: every pack but `lemmings/` uses uppercase `MAIN.DAT` on
  disk — `mainDatFilename()` records the exact case per pack rather than
  guessing/retrying, since a real static-file host is case-sensitive even
  though local dev via `npm run dev` (Vite) on macOS's case-insensitive
  filesystem wouldn't catch a wrong guess; this used to be a
  `mainDatCatalog.js`-local `MAIN_DAT_FILENAME` table, consolidated into
  `gamedataPacks.js`'s shared per-pack table once `gamedataLevelLoader.js`
  needed the same case data for every pack, not just this one module),
  decompresses it via `FileContainer`, and caches
  the result per pack — every subsequent decode from the same pack reuses
  it for free.
- **`decodeFrames(reader, startOffset, count, width, height, bpp, palette, markTransparent = true)`**
  — seeks once, then reads `count` frames sequentially, mirroring
  `Animation.loadFromFile`'s own pattern (used for the walking-
  lemming sprites in section 0) exactly, so multi-frame reads land on the
  correct byte boundaries without needing to hand-compute each frame's
  offset. `markTransparent` exists because the rating signs turned out to
  need the opposite of the usual convention: color-index 0 is genuinely
  used as the signs' black letter-outline color, not as a transparency
  key, and there's no separate "outside the shape" region to protect since
  the whole 72×27 box is meant to fully replace the plaque's rectangle-
  board area underneath it (see `getRatingSignUrl`, below). Marking that
  outline transparent (the default, correct for the plaque frame and every
  scroller asset) instead punched dozens of tiny holes exactly where the
  plaque's own permanently-baked-in "FUN" text sits, which then showed
  through — a jagged, seemingly-doubled outline on whatever rating was
  actually selected. `getRatingSignUrl` passes `false` to opt out and get
  a fully opaque box instead. Confirmed by rendering the decoded sign
  alone against a solid magenta background: with `markTransparent` left on
  (the bug), ~17% of the 144×54 box was transparent; with it off, zero.
- **`frameToCanvas(frame, scale)`** — `Frame.getData()` always reports
  alpha=255 (a "cleared" pixel is opaque black, not transparent — real
  per-pixel transparency lives in the separate `getMask()` array), so this
  rewrites alpha from the mask before compositing, then optionally
  nearest-neighbor upscales (`image-rendering: pixelated` territory) —
  same recipe `converter.html` already uses turning a decoded `Frame` into
  a PNG.
- **`getRatingPlaqueUrl(pack)`**, **`getRatingSignUrl(pack, offset)`**,
  **`getScrollerAssets(pack)`** — the original three exported entry points
  (since joined by `getSoundSignUrl(pack)`/`getSoundIconUrl(pack, state)`
  for the F3 sound sign and `getStatusFontStrip(pack)` for the in-level
  status-bar font — see `src/ui.js`'s section above and the `STATUS_FONT_PART`
  mention below), each
  cached (by pack, or by `pack:offset` for signs), each resolving to a
  `blob:` URL (or, for the scroller, an object of four). Every scroller
  asset gets pre-composited into one wide horizontal strip matching the
  exact layout the old hand-extracted GIF/PNG assets used (768×16 for each
  mechanic, 1504×16 for the 94-glyph font), so `src/scroller.js`'s existing
  `background-position` slicing math needed zero changes.

### Progressive enhancement, not a hard swap

Both `src/menu.js` and `src/scroller.js` keep their old static asset paths
(`RATING_BUTTON_IMAGES`, `img/rating.png`'s CSS `background-image`,
`img/scroller_*.gif`, `img/font_section4_purple_menu.png`) as an **instant
fallback** — shown immediately on first paint — and swap to the live-
decoded `blob:` URL as soon as the async fetch+decode resolves:

- `menu.js`'s `buildRatingVisual()` sets `<img>.src` to the static PNG path
  first (if one exists for that rating), then overwrites it once
  `getRatingSignUrl()`/`getRatingPlaqueUrl()` resolve.
- `scroller.js` injects one shared `<style>` element overriding the
  `.menu-scroller-*` classes' `background-image` once `getScrollerAssets()`
  resolves — cheaper than setting inline styles on the (possibly hundreds
  of) individual glyph `<span>` elements, and it applies automatically to
  every banner instance since it targets the class, not a specific
  element.

If a fetch ever fails (pack missing, network error), both sides just
`console.warn` and quietly keep showing the static fallback — never a
broken image or a thrown error visible to the player.

## Extending this further

Level terrain/objects — once the biggest remaining offline-baked surface —
are now live-decoded for real gameplay too (`src/gamedataLevelLoader.js`,
every rating, including `2-player`), following the same shared per-pack
table (`src/gamedataPacks.js`) the editor's own live decode already used.

**`2-player`'s raw-level gap (described below as it stood before this was
resolved) is now closed.** The local, non-git-tracked `gamedata/amiga/
LemmingsFiles/` was checked (this session's scratch investigation) and
ruled out — it's a WHDLoad installer for the *full* commercial Amiga
*Lemmings*, not a dedicated two-player pack; its level files are
ByteKiller-crunched (an Amiga-native compression scheme, not the DOS
`FileContainer` format this repo's decoder implements), don't
match the fixed-size raw format `converter.html`'s existing
`AMIGA_TWO_PLAYER_CONFIG`/`loadRawTwoPlayerLevel` path expects (2048-byte
`Level NN.lvl` files), and have no confirmed mapping to the 20 levels this
project actually needs — decoding it would have meant writing a ByteKiller
decompressor and parsing the Amiga `Ground{n}`/`Objects{n}` tileset format
from scratch, a real reverse-engineering project. Instead, a genuine
redistributed raw two-player pack (`gamedata/Amiga-Two-Player/` — 20
already-uncompressed `Level NN.lvl` files, exactly matching
`AMIGA_TWO_PLAYER_CONFIG`'s expectations, plus its own copies of
`MAIN.DAT`/`ADLIB.DAT`/`GROUND<n>O.DAT`/`VGAGR<n>.DAT` — proven MD5-identical
to `gamedata/lemmings`'s own) was sourced and added, and
`src/gamedataLevelLoader.js`'s `loadTwoPlayerLevelFromGamedata()` now reads
it directly. See `docs/2-player-dos-assets.md` for the full investigation
and verification (20/20 metadata + geometry match against the previously-
shipped pre-converted output).

Object/decoration *art* (`levels/{gfx,ani,doors,traps}/*.gif`) has also
since been closed for every real pack (`src/groundCatalog.js`'s
`getObjectPieceStrip()` now serves it live via the `liveRef` mechanism —
see `docs/gif-to-gamedata-migration.md`) — the one remaining static-art
dependency is a VGASPEC level's palette-substituted objects, a narrower
gap than what this paragraph originally described.

`ADLIB.DAT`/`TANDYSND.DAT` (once listed above as "not currently decoded")

Every effort is one of three kinds. Prefer A, use B where it unlocks code, and
never let C block A or B.

and the asset decoders.

## Worker loop

```powershell
python tools/behavior.py
python tools/readable.py      # readable view with reviewed names -> build/readable/
python tools/grinder.py facts TARGET
python tools/behavioral.py TARGET SOURCE        # byte-return widening only; isolated

# Promote the unchanged candidate after reviewing the exact result:
python tools/check_function.py TARGET build/workers/NAME/candidate.c --profile aztec36
# Every proof class publishes through one CLI (registry: tools/acceptance.py):
python tools/promote.py CLASS MANIFEST --verify-only   # functions, asm, data, code_data, behavioral, dead_code, mixed
python tools/promote.py CLASS MANIFEST                 # publish: tiered gate, then census and accounting refresh
```

Workers are Codex sessions (`build/workers/NAME`) or Agent subagents. Each
gets one target and a task card, as AGENTS.md describes. The supervisor owns
all canonical writes. Read `docs/COMPILER_LEARNINGS.md` before writing C.

```powershell
python tools/census.py --write
python tools/census.py --check
python tools/hybrid_image.py --check
python -m pytest tests -n 16 --dist=loadscope -m "not regression_serial" -q
python -m pytest tests -m regression_serial -q
```

`build/worker-jobs` (producer jobs found by receipt hash). Prune neither.
A cold cache means re-running the WinUAE worker.

Gate cost is a first-class concern. A strict derivation re-validates every
accepted proof from scratch, and many tests run one against the real
repository. Profile with `--durations` before adding another real-repo test.
Prefer synthetic fixtures for mechanism tests. Keep real-repo replays to the
few that guard canonical results.

Each accepted proof's validation is memoized under ignored
`build/validation-memo/` (`tools/validation_memo.py`). A row is reused only
when every file its validator read, its explicit context and the validator's
tools import closure hash identically; any change re-validates. With a warm
memo `census --check` takes about 14 s (148 s cold) and `hybrid_image.py
--check` about 34 s (147 s cold). The memo is JSON only and is safe to delete.

producer job is audited once per validation scope, not once per provider
(DATA class cold: about 2 h to 7.4 s); `game_image.game()` returns the
fixture-locked image without a census derivation; publishers hash the input
closure once per validated stage instead of around every read; the DATA
snapshot identity handles each batch once (20.3 s to 3.8 s per call). A DATA
verification pass went from 1 h 41 min to 84 s and `check_function --isolated`
from about 60 s to 18 s. Compiles go through `tools/vamos_backend.py`

items and the whole-game link, about 4x faster per compile and parallel;

cache keys embed the source hash of `compiler_oracle.py`
(`same_overlay_export_extractor_sha256`, resident interface
producer/extractor). Editing that file therefore re-keys overlay trials and
stales the ov04 padding recipe (run `tools/padding_refresh.py`, about 1 min).
The cached-artifact gate now treats these hashes as provenance, because
exact re-extraction runs on every read. Dropping them from new identities
would re-key the whole compile cache once. Do that only together with a
planned cache rebuild.

## Retired 2026-10-16

- The per-batch ASM promoters `promote_driver_asm.py`,
  `promote_callback_asm.py` and `promote_frameless_asm.py`. They are replaced

# Tentang proyek ini

## Apa yang sebenarnya dikerjakan

Sebuah gim DOS tahun 1985 dibongkar sampai byte terakhirnya, lalu dibangun ulang —
sekarang menjadi **tiga hal yang berbeda tujuan**:

| | pertanyaannya | jawabannya |
|---|---|---|
| **`src_c/`** | apakah kodenya terbaca benar? | `.EXE` hasil kompilasi **byte-identical** dgn biner 1985 |
| **`port/`** | apakah *aturannya* dipahami? | tulis ulang dalam Python, **1.565/1.565 bingkai identik** |
| **`remake/`** | bisakah pemahaman itu jadi gim yang bebas disebarkan? | ⏳ sedang dibangun, dgn aset baru sepenuhnya |

Ketiganya menjawab pertanyaan yang berbeda, dan itu disengaja. Rekonstruksi yang cocok
byte-per-byte membuktikan **pembacaan**; ia tidak membuktikan **pemahaman** — sebuah
program bisa disalin sempurna tanpa dimengerti sama sekali. Port yang cocok piksel-per-
piksel membuktikan pemahaman, tapi masih memerlukan berkas gim aslinya. Yang ketiga
melepaskan ketergantungan itu.

## Gimnya

**Creative Contraptions** (1985) — Looking Glass Software untuk Bantam Electronic
Publishing. *Bukan* Looking Glass Studios; kemiripan namanya kebetulan.

Sebuah gim edukasi bergaya Rube Goldberg: pemain menyusun mesin bertingkat dari katrol,
tuas, bidang miring, dan pegas, lalu menjalankan bolanya untuk melihat apakah rantainya
bekerja.

- **Programmer:** Jessie Ragsdale
- **Kompiler:** Microsoft C 1.04 — yaitu Lattice C yang di-rebrand — model memori SMALL,
  `int` 16 bit
- **Tampilan:** CGA mode 4, 320×200, empat warna

Ceritanya lebih lengkap ada di [`GAME_GUIDE.md`](GAME_GUIDE.md).

## Sikap soal hak cipta

**Creative Contraptions © 1985 Bantam Electronic Publishing.** Proyek ini tidak
mengklaim hak apa pun atas gim itu, dan **tidak mendistribusikannya**.

Yang ada di repo ini:

- **kode dan analisis** — hasil membaca program, ditulis sendiri;
- **pengekstrak**, bukan hasil ekstraksi. Berkas gim (`GRAPH`, `MECHS`, `ANIMATE`,
  `MISC`, `CONTRAP`, `DGROUP.bin`) dan font ROM BIOS semuanya di-`.gitignore`. Pengguna
  menyediakan salinannya sendiri.

`src_c/` dan `port/` **memerlukan** salinan gim milikmu untuk dijalankan. `remake/`
tidak — begitu selesai, ia berdiri sendiri dan boleh disebarkan bebas.

Kalau kamu pemegang hak Creative Contraptions dan keberatan dgn apa pun di sini, hubungi
pemilik repo; materi yang dipersoalkan akan dicabut.

## Cara kerja yang dipakai

Satu aturan yang dibayar mahal berkali-kali:

> **Bandingkan ke sumber kebenaran, bukan ke keluaran sendiri.**

Setiap angka di dokumen-dokumen ini berasal dari mengadu hasil dgn gim asli yang
berjalan di emulator, per piksel dan per bingkai. Tidak ada yang berasal dari
"kelihatannya benar".

Tiga pelajaran yang paling sering menggigit, dan ketiganya diceritakan lengkap dgn
kegagalannya di [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md):

1. **Angka yang membaik bukan bukti penjelasannya benar.** Beberapa hipotesis menaikkan
   skor kecocokan dgn alasan yang ternyata keliru.
2. **"Jalur kodenya sama" itu argumen, bukan pengukuran.** Enam kali bagian yang
   dibiarkan tak diuji dgn alasan itu, dan keenamnya memunculkan kesalahan.
3. **Sebelum menyimpulkan "alatnya tidak bisa", periksa alat sendiri.** Sebelas dari
   sebelas kali, "terhalang emulator" ternyata "terhalang stub/hook/urutan tombol
   sendiri".

Aturan yang sama berlaku untuk `remake/`, dgn satu perbedaan penting: di sana tidak ada
gim asli untuk dijadikan pembanding. Yang menggantikannya adalah **spesifikasi tertulis**
dan uji yang menjaga aturan mainnya — lihat [`remake/README.md`](remake/README.md).

## Kredit

- Gim asli: **Jessie Ragsdale** (Looking Glass Software), 1985.
- Pembongkaran, port, dan dokumen: pemilik repo, dibantu Claude Code.
- Alat pihak ketiga (di-`.gitignore`, unduh sendiri): Ghidra, DOSBox-X, Unicorn Engine,
  MS C 1.04 + MASM dari arsip PCjs / Internet Archive.

# SDL3 port: design

Goal (user decision 2026-10-18): one executable that plays DuckTales: The Quest for Gold
on a modern system, built from the recovered source. The port is a thin layer: the
reconstructed game runs unchanged on an emulated Amiga, and the platform below turns what
the game asks of the Amiga into an SDL3 window, input, audio and files. `src/` stays the
recovered program (and keeps building the Amiga executable through `tools/game_build.py`);
port behaviour lives in `port/` and `tools/port_gen.py`, never in `src/`. Same shape as
duke1_recon's port.

## Shape

```
src/ (recovered C, typed DATA providers, CODE-data and reconstructed assembly)
   |  tools/game_build.py materializes the accepted sources into translation units
   |  (entry names, runtime-name bindings, DATA providers, BSS reservations) - the same
   |  input the Amiga oracle build compiles
   |  tools/port_gen.py translates them -> build/port-gen/ (never committed)
   v
ducktales.exe = game (generated) + port/override/ + emulated Amiga (port/*.c) + SDL3
```

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| `port/amiga.h`, `port/os.h` | the contract: the OS structures as the game sees them and the platform functions the OS emulation calls |
| `port/os_*.c`, `port/adf.c` | the emulated Amiga: graphics/layers/intuition calls on a planar bitmap model, exec memory, lists and interrupts, DOS files on `DT1:`/`DT2:` |
| `port/main.c` | the game's clock, record/replay, state dumps, presentation and input (below) |
| `port/override/*.c` | port versions of game functions that reach hardware through raw pointers or swap bytes for the 68000 |
| `tools/asm_port.py`, `port/m68k.*`, `port/paula.c` | the RECONSTRUCTED_ASM modules (audio driver, Paula IRQ handlers, VBlank server) translated instruction by instruction, and the Paula they drive (below) |
| `tools/port_gen.py` | mechanical translation of the staged translation units (below) |

## Same source, mechanical translation

`port_gen.py` translates the staged C units of `game_build.py` (the exact code the
verified Amiga build compiles) so the C stays Aztec C 3.6:

* the data model stays explicit: `int` -> `int16_t`, `unsigned` -> `uint16_t`, `short` ->
  `int16_t`, `long` -> `int32_t`; `char` stays as Aztec has it (signed);
* the port is a **32-bit (i686) build**, so pointers stay 4 bytes and records that hold
  pointers keep the Amiga layout; structures use the Amiga's 2-byte alignment;
* absolute hardware accesses (`*(unsigned short *)0xdff004`, `0xbfe0fe` ...) become
  `amiga_read16/amiga_write16(address)` calls into the emulated chips;
* OS glue calls (`F_h00_8A46` = BltBitMap ...) bind to the platform functions of the same
  OS names; c.lib runtime members (`strcpy`, `sprintf` ...) bind to host libc or to
  `port/` equivalents where Aztec semantics differ (16-bit `int` in `printf` formats);
* typed CODE-data assembly (audio scores, envelopes, selectors) becomes C byte arrays with
  the same big-endian bytes and a relocation list for its pointers.

## Byte order

The 68000 is big-endian, the host little-endian. Values the game computes and stores in C
variables are host order and need nothing. Byte order matters only where bytes enter or
leave the game as data:

* binary records read from `DT1:`/`DT2:` files into typed structures (the archive loader's
  binary record kind, `.as` sample headers) - converted where they are loaded, per record
  type, in the platform/override layer;
* CODE-data tables read by the audio driver - kept big-endian and read through `be16/be32`
  in the driver override;
* any access that views a word through a byte pointer (or the reverse). The audit of
  2026-10-18 went through every such view in the generated code once; `port_gen.py`
  handles each kind and lists what it did under `byte_order` in
  `build/port-gen/port-gen-report.json`:

| Kind | Example | Port rule |
|---|---|---|
| `#define` alias inside a scalar | `G_h01_0971` = low byte of the int `G_h01_0970` | `byte_order_aliases`: the offset moves to the host byte |
| separate name inside a scalar | the LZW decoder stores a 16-bit code in `G_h01_A9C2` and reads `G_h01_A9C3`; `A7D8` = low word of the long `A7D6` (7 names) | `access_widths` + `interior_aliases`: every unit's extern declarations give each name's access width; a name inside a wider scalar is placed at the host position of its bits in `data_hunk.c` |
| cast of a scalar's address | `((char *)&i)[1]`, `((int16_t *)&b)[0]` | `scalar_views` -> `BE_VIEW(T, x, k)` (`aztec.h`): `_Generic` flips the index only when `x` is an integer scalar wider than `T` |
| structure naming one byte of a word | ov10 cave cells `{char pad; char bits;}` over an int; ov11 animation descriptors read byte +5 of the int `word4` | `WORD_BYTE_PAIRS` (reviewed list): the two byte members are swapped |

  Reviewed and left alone: byte arrays used only by address (`motion`, `prefix`, `pad18`
  passed to functions), record tables viewed through different structures with the same
  field widths, `sscanf("%d")` into `Slot.text` (an int written and read as an int),
  `Rec.kind` (bytes everywhere), OS structures (Node, BitMap, Preferences). The game's
  input handler reads byte 7 of an InputEvent (the low byte of `ie_Code`): the platform
  must write the event in that view.

A state dump of the port is the DATA/BSS hunk as the port holds it: original offsets, host
byte order. `tools/game_compare.py --port` reads each typed global of
`recovery/data_model.json` through its type (numbers by value, pointers never), so it
compares directly with WinUAE state dumps.

## Determinism: one clock, inputs at the game's input reads

The port runs everything on the game thread: no timer thread, no audio callback into the
driver, no lock. The game's clock is one tick per PAL frame (71051 colour clocks, 20.0318 ms)
and advances only when the game waits for time (`Delay`, `WaitBOVP`, and busy-waits on
interrupt state). A tick runs, in order, Paula for one frame (its block interrupts run the
driver) and the VBlank servers. Live play paces ticks to real time; `--headless` does not.

What reaches the game from outside (measured from the code, 2026-10-18):

| Input | Where | In the replay log |
|---|---|---|
| joystick and fire | `poll_controller_and_keyboard_input` reads JOY1DAT and CIA-A PRA | `joy`, `fire` |
| keys | the input handler (`input.device`), drained by the same poll | `key` (raw code, bit 7 = release) |
| RNG seed | `seed_random` stores VPOSR + `game_frame_tick` | `seed` (the stored value) |
| time | `Delay`, `WaitBOVP`; busy-waits on the audio driver's channel-0 state `G_h01_2A16` ("until the sound ends") and on `game_frame_tick` | the clock itself |

Nothing else in the game reads interrupt-driven state. VPOSR holds LOF (bit 15) and V8 (bit
0), not the line number, so the seed is 0x8000 + `game_frame_tick` (+1): the frames spent
before the difficulty choice.

**The time base: poll frames.** The 68000 spends frames drawing, decompressing and loading;
the port spends none. Inputs timed in frames therefore reach the two machines in different
states. Inputs, checkpoints and the end of a replay are instead timed in *poll frames*, the
steps of the game's own input reading: a poll starts a new poll frame when the game has waited
for time (`Delay`, `WaitBOVP`) since the current one began, or when it also polled in the frame
just before (a loop polling every frame while a sound plays). Work that spans frames does not,
on either machine. The port counts them in `platform_poll` (called by the first input register
the poll reads - it reads the fire bit before JOY1DAT); `tools/game_boot.py` counts them on
the original with breakpoints at the poll, `Delay`/`WaitBOVP` glue and the VBlank server (below).
Busy-waits get one frame per pass from `port_gen.py` (`spin_waits`; a loop whose body already
waits keeps its own pace) through `platform_spin_frame`, which is not a game wait.

The port runs the recovered input poll and `seed_random` unchanged: `port_gen.py` turns their
16-bit dereferences of custom chip and CIA addresses into `amiga_read16`, so JOY1DAT, CIA-A PRA
and VPOSR are register reads of the emulated chips (`hardware_reads`). Replay hands VPOSR the
recorded seed minus the game clock, so `seed_random` computes the recorded seed itself.

Addresses are run-independent: AllocMem and the OS structures the game sees come from one
fixed arena with exec's algorithm, the executable has a fixed base, and the DATA hunk owns every
cell the runtime knows by name (`_numdev`, `GfxBase`, `DOSBase`, `_argc` ...: `RUNTIME_CELLS`)
and every link-only stub cell. Guest memory is registered (`m68k_memory`); an access outside it
is a verification fault (`platform_fault`): logged, exit status 3, and `--strict` stops the run.

`ducktales --record FILE` / `--replay FILE` (text, poll frames):

```
# from tools/game_boot.py: WinUAE inputs at the poll frame that read them
1015 fire 0001
1016 fire 0000
0 seed 8000
0 seed 8aa6
1 sound 0001
1015 sound 0000
1082 end
```

`sound` lines (the sound commands the game issued) are events for comparison; replay ignores
them. `--dump DIR:FROM:EVERY` dumps the DATA/BSS hunk at the first poll of every EVERY-th poll
frame, with the guest regions in `state-layout.json`; `--shot FILE.bmp:TICK`; `--ticks N`.

**The original and the build, driven the same way.** `tools/game_boot.py run --poll-dumps N`
drives WinUAE by events instead of frame steps: it runs to the next watched entry - the input
poll, `seed_random`, `play_sound`, the `Delay`/`WaitBOVP` glue, the VBlank server - and acts
there: at a poll that starts a poll frame it injects the inputs due (the poll reads them at
once - measured: fire injected at the entry is in the poll's result), counts it and dumps every
N-th; at `seed_random` it takes (or pins) the seed exactly; at `play_sound` it records the
command. Frames without polls run at emulation speed. (A frame step cannot do this: with a
breakpoint armed, WinUAE's frame steps run past their target line, and its memory watches do
not fire during frame steps; debugger stops do not change the emulation.) With `--input` (a
frame-stamped script) a run writes `port-replay.log`; with `--replay LOG` it is driven by a log,
so one log drives the original, a build and the port.

## Verification: what is proven, and how to find the first divergence

Measured 2026-10-18 with `evidence/trace/title-to-money-bin.json` (title, office, Money Bin,
difficulty choice, company/location setup, contest screen; 6,000 emulated frames = 1,082 poll
frames, turbo floppy). One log, `title-to-money-bin.poll.log`, recorded from the original,
drives all three machines.

| Claim | Evidence | Result |
|---|---|---|
| The original replays identically across fresh WinUAE sessions | fixed emulated start (`START_CCK`), frame-stepped and poll-driven runs | identical: CPU and beam on every frame, every dump, the same seeds; three poll-driven sessions wrote the same log |
| The log replays the original exactly | the original driven by its own poll-keyed log (`--replay`) | the round trip reproduces the log: same inputs, poll frames, seeds, sound commands |
| The port replays exactly | the log replayed twice; a live run recorded and replayed | byte-identical: 1,082 dumps (one per poll frame) and screenshots |
| Original vs SDL3 port | the log, a dump at every poll frame (`game_compare.py --port --events`) | **sound commands 23/23 identical (same commands, same poll frames); 1,009 of 1,018 typed globals identical at all 1,082 checkpoints.** The other nine are the audio driver's state (below) |
| Original vs reconstructed Amiga build | the log (`--replay`), every 25th poll frame | sound commands 23/23 identical; 964 of 978 globals identical at all 42 checkpoints; the rest are pointers (compared by value - the build's link layout differs) and the same audio-driver state |
| A wrong rule is caught and located | mutation `% 37` to `% 36` in the treasure assignment (port) | against the original: exactly `location_records` and `location_treasure_slots` differ, from poll frame 1,054 (the first poll after the reseed that shuffles them) to the end; everything else as before |
| A replay proves only what it runs | mutation `>= 35` to `> 35` in `wrap_location_index` | not exercised by this script: no difference |

How the comparison reads state (`tools/game_compare.py`): every typed global of
`recovery/data_model.json` through its type - numbers by value (the port's in host order),
pointers by what they point at (an offset in the DATA hunk, the one region both machines lay
out alike), two addresses elsewhere as *incomparable* (listed, never counted as a match),
a number never as an address; the three dos.library file handles as open/closed; the Aztec CLI
startup's argument cells and device table (`_argc`, `_argv` ...) listed as launch environment,
since the port starts without a CLI. Every category is printed in the report.

What still differs, and why:

* **The audio driver's own state** (block countdowns, sample cursors, the channel-0 stream
  pointer): audio advances with real frames, and at the same poll frame the original has spent
  more frames (its work between polls), so its sounds are further along. The sound commands the
  game issues are identical; what the game reads back - "has the sound ended", in busy-waits - did
  not change any game state in this script. A test that waits on a sound with work in the loop
  body would show it.
* **Load-time and work-time are not modelled**, by design: the port does instantly what takes
  the 68000 frames. Gameplay that counts loop passes *until a sound ends* (an animation that
  runs while a tune plays) can make more passes in the port; this script has none that change
  state.

Finding the first divergence: replay the log on both, `game_compare.py ORIG PORT --port` with a
dump at every poll frame (`--poll-dumps 1`, `--dump .:1:1`), take the earliest global that
differs at every lag, then the function that writes it - against the original 68000 code with
`tools/difftest.py` where it is a single function. Found this way so far: the envelope table
bound to an older compact copy in the build (sound 6 read data as a pointer), Paula raising its
start interrupt too early (the driver lost one block count), the fire bit read before the poll
frame started (a press seen one poll late), a busy-wait rule stretching loops that already
wait, and runtime cells (`_numdev`, the library bases) living outside the DATA hunk.

Recording a human playthrough: play the original in WinUAE with `game_boot.py` or the port
with `--record`; the poll-keyed log replays on the original, the build and the port. Recording
in the original is the reference: its log is the input the other two must reproduce.

## From compatibility port to native game

What each part of the port is for (A game logic and state, B a platform interaction the game
needs, C compatibility with a historical implementation detail, D reconstruction and
verification only), and how it leaves:

| Part | Kind | What the game gets from it | Route out |
|---|---|---|---|
| generated game C (`src/` through `port_gen.py`) | A | the game | becomes the native source module by module: a readable rewrite of one subsystem, proven equal by replay, replaces its generated units |
| the game clock in `main.c` (this change) | A | the fixed 50 Hz update the game is paced by | stays: it is the native game loop; rendering and audio can run at their own rates around it |
| `data_hunk.c` (DATA/BSS at original offsets) | C | the game indexes across separately declared globals and keeps addresses in state | typed state structures once `recovery/data_model.json` covers the indexed tables |
| `os_graphics.c` (planar bitmaps, minterm blits, copper View) | B | drawing into bitplanes, palette through copper lists | semantic draw calls (sprite with mask, rectangle copy, text, palette set) where the game's call sites show the meaning; checked by per-tick screenshot equality under replay |
| `paula.c`, translated driver (`asm_port.py`, `m68k.*`) | B + C | music and effects through a 68000 driver on emulated Paula | a native C driver once its behaviour is pinned by WAV equality per replay; the driver's state feeds back into the game only through the "sound finished" busy-waits |
| `os_exec.c` (arena, lists, ports, interrupts) | C | exec semantics the game relies on (its own MemHeader pool, interrupt servers) | goes with the code that calls it |
| `os_dos.c`, `adf.c` | B | files from the two disks | host files (the extracted assets) |
| `runtime.c` (`segload` no-op), overrides | C | overlays, Aztec startup/exit, the blitter plane union, little-endian file fields | the input poll and `seed_random` overrides are gone (2026-10-18: the recovered functions run unchanged, their hardware reads go to the emulated chips); the rest go when their callers are rewritten |
| record/replay, dumps, guest-memory checks | D | nothing | stays as the verification harness, outside the game proper |

Removed so far: the timer thread, the audio-callback interrupts and the driver lock (one
thread, a fixed order: the port became reproducible); the hand-written copies of the input poll
and `seed_random` (91 + 15 lines: the recovered functions run unchanged, with hardware reads
translated by `port_gen.py`); the port's separate definitions of runtime cells (the DATA hunk
owns them).

## Build

CMake + SDL3 3.4.16, Windows first: MinGW-w64 **i686** gcc (`C:/msys64/mingw32`) and the
SDL3 MinGW package (`C:/tools/sdl3-3.4.16-mingw/SDL3-3.4.16/i686-w64-mingw32`).
`port_gen.py` runs as a build step after `game_build.py --stage`.

## Status

2026-10-18: `tools/port_gen.py` translates all 653 C units of the Amiga build's compile
plan; 651 compile with i686 gcc without errors (two need port versions: the Aztec `_main`
startup and `_exit`, both with inline 68000 assembly; four more reach custom chips or the
CIA through raw addresses). The materialization assembly (1,450 measured BSS reservations,
symbol aliases) becomes `materialization.s`, and every DATA/BSS symbol then resolves. A
trial link leaves 133 undefined names - the platform surface:

* about 70 OS calls (exec, dos, graphics, layers, intuition, icon) and the library bases;
* the Aztec runtime pieces the game binds by name (`segload`/`freeseg` overlay loading -
  a no-op here, everything is linked - `movmem`, `index`, `argc`/`argv`, `devtab`, `errno`);
* about 50 entry points of the reconstructed assembly (audio driver, Paula interrupt
  handlers, VBlank server and callbacks) and the CODE-data tables they read;
* one unrecovered code fragment (`F_h00_4692`) and the startup/exit versions.

Later on 2026-10-18 the port links and runs (port/README.md): it boots through the
office scene with the original graphics, copper palette and text. Found the hard way:

| Amiga behaviour | What went wrong | Where it is reproduced |
|---|---|---|
| the game indexes across DATA providers (`G_h01_27E4[n]` runs into `27E8`...) | separate C globals: wrong cells, crash | `data_hunk.c`: the whole DATA/BSS hunk as one structure at original offsets |
| the game carves blocks from its own MemHeader pool and checks them on free | host-heap blocks: BAD POINTER, shutdown | exec `Allocate`/`Deallocate` on the MemHeader |
| `request_disk` walks DOSBase->dl_Root->rn_Info->di_DevInfo | NULL DOSBase: crash | `dos_init`: DosLibrary, RootNode, DosInfo, volume nodes |
| little-endian file fields are swapped in memory for the 68000 | `LoadIT() - Unknown block type` | `override/resident_F_2D66.c`, `2DBA.c`: assemble the value from bytes |
| VBlank colour cycling writes into the copper list | (would freeze the palette) | `MrgCop` builds the colour MOVEs at the layout it expects |
| a byte alias names the low byte of a big-endian `int` (`G_h01_0971` = low byte of `G_h01_0970`, the bitplane depth) | every sprite BitMap got Depth 0: no sprites, no speech bubbles | `port_gen.byte_order_aliases`: narrower views inside scalars move to the host byte |
| BltMaskBitMapRastPort indexes its minterm as source, mask, destination (0xE2 = cookie-cut) | (sprites would have been OR'd onto the background) | `F_h00_4692` in `os_graphics.c` |
| byte views of words elsewhere: 7 interior names, 4 address casts, cave cells, animation descriptors (byte-order audit above) | (would have broken the LZW decoder, the ov10 cave and the ov11 animations) | `port_gen` byte-order rules |

## The reconstructed assembly, translated

`tools/asm_port.py` (run by `port_gen.py`) translates the RECONSTRUCTED_ASM modules - the
audio driver, the four Paula interrupt handlers, the VBlank server and its colour
callbacks - and the TYPED_CODE_DATA tables (scores, envelopes, selectors) mechanically, so
the port plays the reconstructed driver itself rather than a rewrite of it:

* every instruction becomes one labelled C statement on the register file of
  `port/m68k.h`, with the condition codes the following branch reads;
* original addresses come from instruction sizes and the assembler's span-dependent
  branch sizes, plus two Manx rules found in the build's bytes: a `public` declared
  outside `dseg` is addressed `d16(a4)`, and `jsr label` assembles PC-relative. Every
  address-named label and every label in `build/game/DuckTales.sym` (700) is checked
  against the computed layout;
* a code address is `M68K_CODE_BASE` + its original offset. The DATA hunk's jump tables
  (`recon_h00_544C + 200`) and the Interrupt structures hold these keys and
  `m68k_run()` dispatches them; the five entries the C code calls get C wrappers that
  push their arguments as Aztec C does;
* memory is host-order (the DATA hunk and heap hold what the C code wrote), except the
  tables, which keep their big-endian bytes (32-bit references patched in at start), and
  0xDFF000-0xDFF1FF, the custom chips (`port/paula.c`);
* one lock serializes the driver's entries from the game thread, the VBlank timer, the
  audio callback (Paula's block interrupts) and the input handler, as one CPU did.

Paula starts with DMA and interrupts master-enabled, as the OS leaves them; the driver
never sets those bits itself. With the driver running, the title screen stays until its
tune ends (about 66 seconds) before the office scene, as on the Amiga; the silent stub
had skipped that wait.

Known difference: the build's audio tables still miss about 200 bytes of RAW_ORACLE_DEBT
inside typed scores and envelopes (for example 26 bytes in `score_1836` at original
0x19F8, which the build leaves out, shifting what follows) and about 420 typed-table bytes
differ from the original (`build/game/diff.json`). Some tunes or effects can play
differently from the original until those spans are recovered as typed data.

Record/replay and the verification canary: above (2026-10-18). Next: inputs timed by consumption, then wider scripts (docs/NEXT.md).
